html:
The Holocaust was the murder of about six million European Jews by Nazi Germany and its helpers between 1941 and 1945, during World War II. Persecution began earlier, in 1933, when Adolf Hitler took power: laws stripped Jews of their rights, a pogrom in 1938 burned synagogues, and many fled, among them Sigmund Freud.

Mass killing began with the invasion of the Soviet Union in 1941, when mobile squads shot Jews by the hundreds of thousands. From 1942 the regime sent Jews from all over occupied Europe by train to death camps in occupied Poland, among them Auschwitz, Treblinka and Sobibor, where most were gassed on arrival. The Nazis also murdered the Roma, disabled people, Soviet prisoners and many Poles.

Polish Jewry, the largest Jewish community in Europe since the Statute of Kalisz drew Jews east, was almost wiped out, and with it much of the Hasidic world. Anne Frank, hiding in Amsterdam, was betrayed and died in Bergen-Belsen in 1945; her diary became the best known witness.

After the war Nazi leaders were tried at Nuremberg, the word genocide entered law, and Europe built new protections such as the European Convention on Human Rights. The Holocaust also strengthened the case for a Jewish state, and Israel was founded in 1948.
